# Updated model fitted with `spBayes`

Compared to the [previous version](https://public.websites.umich.edu/~jializ/urban-phe/workflow_validate_spmodel_WU.html#mcmc-1), I have updated the following parts:

-   Update spatial random effect model fitted with `spBayes`. The updates include corrections to the previously unsuitable knots settings and adjustments to the prior settings in the model.

-   Replaced the temperature data source with U-HAT, a seamless 1-km gridded dataset, instead of the previous station-based observations.

-   Increased the sample size by incorporating more individual phenology records.

-   Models were fitted separately for each species.


In terms of coefficients in [@fig-sp-mcmc], the results are similar to those from other models. However, in `spBayes`, I couldn't find a method to specify the random effect for the `year`, so it was treated as a fixed categorical effect. Additionally, the WAIC values became difficult to compare, being 10 times larger than those from other models (which may be due to the WAIC calculation function I set up myself). But, I believe the model fit is reasonable in general.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Helper to process files by pattern

generate_mcmc_plot <- function(dir_path, coef, fixed_sp){
  process_files <- function(file_list, phe_type_label) {
    param_list <- map(file_list, function(file) {
      model_data <- readRDS(file)
      genus <- sub(paste0("(.*?)_", phe_type_label, "\\.rds"), "\\1", basename(file))
      param_data <- ggs(model_data$samples) |>
          filter(str_starts(Parameter, fixed(coef))) |>
          rename(ParameterOriginal = Parameter) |>
          mutate(Parameter = genus)|>
          mutate(converge = model_data$converge)

      return(param_data)
    })
    combined_param_data <- bind_rows(param_list) |>
      mutate(phe_type = phe_type_label)
    return(combined_param_data)
}
  # Collect files
  SOS_files <- list.files(dir_path, pattern = "SOS\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)
  EOS_files <- list.files(dir_path, pattern = "EOS\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)

  # Process each type
  if (length(SOS_files) == 0) {
    sos_data <- NULL
  } else {
  sos_data <- process_files(SOS_files, "SOS")
  }
  if (length(EOS_files) == 0) {
    eos_data <- NULL
  } else {
    eos_data <- process_files(EOS_files, "EOS")
  }

  combined_param_data <- bind_rows(sos_data, eos_data)
  combined_param_data$phe_type <- factor(combined_param_data$phe_type, levels = c("SOS", "EOS"))

  # Summarize
  summary_data <- combined_param_data |>
    group_by(Parameter, phe_type) |>
    summarise(
      median_value = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      lower_2_5 = quantile(value, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
      upper_97_5 = quantile(value, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
      converge = first(converge),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(Sig = ifelse(lower_2_5 * upper_97_5 > 0, "*", ""),
           SigAlpha = ifelse(Sig == "*", 1, 0.2),
           Color = ifelse(median_value >0, "#0D0887FF" , "#FCA636FF")) 

  param_levels <- rev(unique(summary_data$Parameter))

  # Plot
  
  p1 <- ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = factor(as.character(Parameter), levels = param_levels), y = median_value,
                                 colour = Color)) +
    geom_point(aes(alpha = SigAlpha), size=3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_2_5, ymax = upper_97_5, alpha = SigAlpha), width = 0.4) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(median_value, 3)),
              vjust = -0.7, size = 3) +
    scale_alpha_identity() +
    scale_color_identity() +
    guides(alpha = "none") +
    facet_wrap(~ phe_type, scales = "free_x") +  # flip x/y means free_x
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate") +
    theme(
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14)
    ) +
      coord_flip()
  p2 <- ggplot(combined_param_data |> filter(Parameter %in% c("Tilia_tomentosa", "Ulmus_americana")), aes(x = value)) +
    geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~ Parameter, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
      x = paste0("Posterior distribution of ", coef),
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    facet_grid(Parameter ~ phe_type, scales = "free_y")+
    # geom_text(data = summary_data, aes(x = median_value-3, y = 0, label = round(median_value, 3)), vjust = -1, size = 3) +
    geom_text(data = summary_data |> filter(Parameter %in% c("Tilia_tomentosa", "Ulmus_americana")), aes(x = median_value+3, y = 0, label = paste0("gelman.diag: ", round(converge, 4))), vjust = -1, color = "red", size = 2) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_blank(),
      strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0),
      panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines")
    )
  
  p <- list(coef_summary_plot = p1, coef_density_plot = p2, summary_data = summary_data)
  return(p)
}

mcmc_semi_matern <- function(r_output_dir, phe_type) {
  plots_mean <- list()
  plots_semi <- list()
  # Load the data
  r_files <- list.files(r_output_dir, pattern = paste0(phe_type, "\\.rds$"), full.names = TRUE)
  for (file in r_files) {
    model_data <- readRDS(file)
    taxon <- sub(paste0("(.*?)_", phe_type, "\\.rds"), "\\1", basename(file))
    surf_sf <- model_data$surf_sf
    CorDF <- model_data$CorDF
    r <- raster(extent(surf_sf), resolution = 1000)
    raster_field <- rasterize(surf_sf, r, field = "w_mean")
    raster_df <- as.data.frame(raster_field, xy = TRUE)
    plot_spatial_field <- ggplot(raster_df) +
      geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = layer)) +
      scale_fill_viridis(na.value = "transparent") +
      coord_fixed(ratio = 0.8) +
      ggtitle(paste(taxon)) +
      labs(fill = "E[w|data]") +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6, angle = 45, hjust = 1),
            plot.title = element_text(size = 8))
        
    plot_cor <- ggplot(CorDF, aes(x = Distance, y = Median)) +
      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), fill = "grey", alpha = 0.4) +
      geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
      labs(x = "Distance (m)", y = "Correlation", title = "Matern Correlation Function") +
      ggtitle(paste(taxon)) +
      theme_minimal()+
      theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6, angle = 45, hjust = 1),
            plot.title = element_text(size = 8))
        
    plots_mean[[taxon]] <- plot_spatial_field
    plots_semi[[taxon]] <- plot_cor
  }
  combined_plot_mean <- wrap_plots(plots_mean, ncol = 5)
  combined_plot_semi <- wrap_plots(plots_semi, ncol = 5)
  
   return(list(
    combined_plot_semi = combined_plot_semi,
    combined_plot_mean = combined_plot_mean
  ))
}

```

Next, I updated the spatial field and covariance function fitted with `spBayes`. Using the Genus - Start of Season (SOS) as an example, some genera (such as Juglans, Quercus and Ulmus) show very small ranges, exhibiting noisy patterns in spatial fields. Other genera, on the other hand, show smoother spatial patterns. This might be due to differences in sample sizes or inherent differences in spatial variability between species/genera.

Compared to the results from INLA below ([@fig-ny-inla-plot_semi]), the two covariance functions differ, but the magnitude of the spatial random effect is similar. Additionally, `spBayes` avoids the extreme values seen in Platanus. The Alnus, Carya and Salix were not included in the `spBayes` fitting because they have very small sample sizes, which leads to unreliable estimates.

# Detailed response

> you could smooth the temperature surface to create a predictor without having to specify the 500m radius around stations, which is somewhat arbitrary

Do you mean using interpolation? That would be feasible in this project. But I am curious if we reconstruct the temperature surface using some covariance structure, would that compete with the random spatial effect in the model and potentially affect the inference? I also have a raster-based temperature product as an alternative. But that raster is itself built from spatial autocorrelation, so I’m concerned it could have the same kind of overlap with the spatial random effect.

> what is the sample size?

It depends on the species or genus, ranging from over 30 unique points to as many as 300.

> to me it's unclear what the fixed effects without correlation represent. I'm not sure what you mean

Based on the grouping information from the hexagon cell, these groups are directly included in the model as a categorical variable. I included this to compare with model 3, where grouping variable is used as a random effect. For models using the hexagon grouping, no additional spatial random effect was included.

> you mention hexagonal grid cells but earlier it looked like you had point-referenced data. so it's a bit unclear: if you have cells, do you aggregate the data on trees?

The hexagon cells only provide grouping information for point-referenced data; they do not aggregate the data.

> you split the trees into genus, but you did not mention that earlier. do you run the analysis separately for each genus or are you using genus as a covariate? unclear

For each genus and species, I ran the analysis separately.

> you mention matern covariance -- do you estimate all parameters including the smoothness? if not, what did you fix the smoothness to? you should also mention how you chose the prior for the spatial range

In spBayes, I estimated all covariance parameters ($\phi$, $\sigma^2$, $\tau^2$, and $\nu$) in the Matérn model, with $\nu$ (smoothness) assigned a $\text{Uniform}(0.5, 2.5)$ prior and the spatial range $\phi$ was assigned a prior based on the maximum distance, specifically, $\phi \sim \text{Unif}(\frac{3}{0.75*\text{max.d}}, \frac{3}{0.001*\text{max.d}})$. In INLA, the SPDE model uses vague Gaussian priors on the log-precision parameters $\theta$ (mean 0, precision 0.1), with the prior median range heuristically set to about 20% of the mesh diameter, so the effective prior depends on the chosen mesh. The smoothness ($\nu$) is fixed at 1 by default.

> figure 6 is very odd, with some panels being essentially constant and the scales being all over the place. check what's going on

[@fig-ny-spbayes-plot_semi] is the updated version. Some genera (such as Juglans, Quercus and Ulmus) show very small ranges, exhibiting noisy patterns in spatial fields. Other genera, on the other hand, show smoother spatial patterns. This might be due to differences in sample sizes or inherent differences in spatial variability between species/genera.

> figure 10 mentions a hexagonal grid -- is this what you mentioned earlier? so you'd be assuming a piecewise constant intercept on the grid, with no spatial autocorrelation across grid points? it remains unclear what you mean by random vs fixed effects with respect to what you say in 2.4

Yes, figure 10 refers to the hexagonal grid, which provides grouping information for the point-referenced data. And I considered 2 alternative spatial effect based on this grid:

-   Random group effect: treating the hexagon cell as a grouping factor with a random intercept (a form of spatial random effect, but without explicit covariance between cells).

-   Fixed group effect: treating the hexagon cell as a set of fixed intercepts, i.e. piecewise constant baseline values for each cell, with no spatial autocorrelation across cells.

> you make correlation plots for inla but not for spBayes, but you can do that too

[@fig-ny-spbayes-plot_semi] is the updated version. Compared to the results from INLA ([@fig-ny-inla-plot_semi]), the two covariance functions differ, but the magnitude of the spatial random effect is similar. Additionally, `spBayes` avoids the extreme values seen in Platanus.

> there seems to be a disconnect between mcmc/inla and models. I would have guessed they should agree: if the spatial covariance model is better, it should be better regardless of what algorithm is used to fit it. so I would definitely double check your implementation in spBayes

I had the same expectation. I have updated the MCMC implementation in spBayes to rule out issues with the model implementation. The current results show that, the estimates of coefficients are similar to those from other models ([@fig-sp-mcmc]). However, in `spBayes` I couldn’t find a way to specify a random effect for year, so I treated it as a fixed categorical effect. I am not planning to use a full spatio-temporal model since the number of temporal slices is limited (7–8 years).

In addition, when comparing model metrics, I found that the updated model’s WAIC values became difficult to compare, about 10 times larger than those from other models (possibly due to the bugs in my WAIC calculation function). But overall, I believe the model fit is reasonable.

Do you have any suggestions on how best to handle the `year` variable in spBayes, or on more reliable ways to compare models in this context?
